<header class="dg-head dg-head-section"><p class="dg-kicker">Appendix B <span class="dg-sep">•</span> <a href="index.html">Proofs &amp; Comments</a></p><h1 class="dg-title"><span class="dg-secnum">B.6</span> Chart-induced basis of <span class="math inline">\(T_p^*\mathcal{M}\)</span> (§<a class="dg-xref" href="../tangent-spaces/cotangent-space.html#subsection_Basis_and_Coordinate_Components_of_TstarpM" data-kind="subsection" data-label="subsection_Basis_and_Coordinate_Components_of_TstarpM">4.2.1</a>)</h1></header>
<p>In this appendix, we provide a formal proof that the set of chart-induced covectors <span class="math display">\[
    \left\lbrace (d\mathscr{X}^1)_p,\; \ldots,\; (d\mathscr{X}^d)_p \right\rbrace
\]</span> constitutes a basis for the cotangent space <span class="math inline">\(T_p^*\mathcal{M}\)</span> at a point <span class="math inline">\(p \in \mathcal{M}\)</span>, associated with a given chart <span class="math inline">\((\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X})\)</span> containing <span class="math inline">\(p\)</span>. This amounts to verifying that these elements satisfy the conditions of a basis, additionally, we also show here that this set is the dual basis induced by the tangent basis <span class="math inline">\(\left\lbrace \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^1} \right)_p, \dots, \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^d} \right)_p \right\rbrace\)</span>:</p>
<ul class="dg-itemize dg-depth-1">
<li><p><strong>Duality pairing with the tangent basis:</strong>  First, we recall that the covector <span class="math inline">\((d\mathscr{X}^i)_p\)</span> acts on the chart-induced vector <span class="math inline">\(\left( \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^j} \right)_p\)</span> as:  <span class="math display">\begin{align*}
            (d\mathscr{X}^i)_p \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^j} \right)_p
            &amp;= \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^j} \right)_p (\mathscr{X}^i)
            = \delta^i_j.
        \end{align*}</span>  This holds because the action of <span class="math inline">\(\left( \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^j} \right)_p\)</span> on the coordinate function <span class="math inline">\(\mathscr{X}^i\)</span> yields <span class="math inline">\(1\)</span> if <span class="math inline">\(i = j\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\(0\)</span> otherwise (see Section <a class="dg-xref" href="proof-basis-tpm.html" data-kind="section" data-label="section_proof_basis_TpM">B.5</a>).</p>
<p>This result immediately guarantees that the set <span class="math inline">\(\left\lbrace (d\mathscr{X}^i)_p \right\rbrace\)</span> forms the dual basis to <span class="math inline">\(\left\lbrace \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^j} \right)_p \right\rbrace\)</span>.</p>
<div class="dg-skip dg-medskip"></div></li>
<li><p><strong>Linear independence:</strong>  Suppose that some linear combination of the covectors yields the zero covector:  <span class="math display">\begin{align*}
            0 = \sum_{i=1}^d \alpha_i \cdot (d\mathscr{X}^i)_p, \qquad \alpha_i \in \mathbb{R}.
        \end{align*}</span>  Our goal here is to check if this condition holds only when all the coefficients <span class="math inline">\(\alpha^i\)</span> are zero independently (if so, we will have proven linear independence), or if there exists other possible combinations of the coefficients <span class="math inline">\(\alpha^i\)</span> that also yield the zero vector as a result.</p>
<p>Let this expression act on any arbitrary basis vector <span class="math inline">\(\left( \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^j} \right)_p\)</span>:  <span class="math display">\begin{align*}
            0 &amp;= \left( \sum_{i=1}^d \alpha_i \cdot (d\mathscr{X}^i)_p \right)
            \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^j} \right)_p
            = \sum_{i=1}^d \alpha_i \cdot
            (d\mathscr{X}^i)_p \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^j} \right)_p
            = \sum_{i=1}^d \alpha_i \cdot \delta^i_j = \alpha_j.
        \end{align*}</span>  Since this holds for arbitrary <span class="math inline">\(j = 1, \dots, d\)</span>, it immediately follows that <span class="math inline">\(\alpha_j = 0\)</span> for all <span class="math inline">\(j\)</span>. Therefore, the set <span class="math inline">\(\left\lbrace (d\mathscr{X}^i)_p \right\rbrace\)</span> is linearly independent.</p>
<div class="dg-skip dg-medskip"></div></li>
<li><p><strong>Spanning:</strong>  Let <span class="math inline">\(\mathsf{X} \in T_p^*\mathcal{M}\)</span> be an arbitrary covector. Since <span class="math inline">\(\mathsf{X}\)</span> is a linear map on <span class="math inline">\(T_p\mathcal{M}\)</span>, its action is fully determined by its values on the basis vectors <span class="math inline">\(\left( \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^i} \right)_p\)</span>. These values are real numbers:  <span class="math display">\begin{align*}
            \mathtt{x}^i \coloneqq \mathsf{X} \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^i} \right)_p
            \in \mathbb{R}, \qquad \forall i = 1, \dots, d.
        \end{align*}</span>  We call these the <span class="dg-term dg-term-blue">covector components</span> of <span class="math inline">\(\mathsf{X}\)</span> in the chart <span class="math inline">\((\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X})\)</span>.</p>
<p>We now claim that the covector  <span class="math display">\begin{align*}
            \tilde{\mathsf{X}} \coloneqq \sum_{i=1}^d
            \mathtt{x}^i \cdot (d\mathscr{X}^i)_p
        \end{align*}</span>  coincides with <span class="math inline">\(\mathsf{X}\)</span>.</p>
<p>Let us verify that <span class="math inline">\(\tilde{\mathsf{X}}\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\(\mathsf{X}\)</span> agree upon acting on any vector <span class="math inline">\(v_{\gamma,p} \in T_p\mathcal{M}\)</span>. Applying <span class="math inline">\(\tilde{\mathsf{X}}\)</span> to <span class="math inline">\(v_{\gamma,p}\)</span>:  <span class="math display">\begin{align*}
            \tilde{\mathsf{X}}(v_{\gamma,p})
            &amp;= \left( \sum_{i=1}^d
            \mathtt{x}^i \cdot (d\mathscr{X}^i)_p \right) (v_{\gamma,p})
            = \sum_{i=1}^d
            \mathtt{x}^i \cdot (d\mathscr{X}^i)_p (v_{\gamma,p})
            = \sum_{i=1}^d
            \mathtt{x}^i \cdot (d\mathscr{X}^i)_p
            \left( \sum_{j=1}^d \dot{\gamma}^j(\lambda_0) \cdot
            \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^j} \right)_p \right) \\
            &amp;= \sum_{i=1}^d
            \mathtt{x}^i \cdot
            \left[ \sum_{j=1}^d \dot{\gamma}^j(\lambda_0)
            \cdot \underbrace{(d\mathscr{X}^i)_p \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^j} \right)_p}_{\delta^i_j} \right]
            = \sum_{i=1}^d
            \mathtt{x}^i \cdot \dot{\gamma}^i(\lambda_0)
            = \mathsf{X} \left( \sum_{i=1}^d \dot{\gamma}^i(\lambda_0) \cdot
            \left( \frac{\partial}{\partial \mathscr{X}^i} \right)_p \right) \\
            &amp;= \mathsf{X}(v_{\gamma,p}). \quad \square
        \end{align*}</span></p></li>
</ul>
